topic: Introduction to Religions (Two from the SL list)
subject: religious-studies

items.title: Aquinas offered Five Ways, not one argument

options.text: Five distinct a posteriori arguments in Summa Theologiae I.2.3: motion (unmoved mover), causation (uncaused cause), contingency (necessary being), degree (greatest being), teleology (designer)

items.reveal:
Aquinas distinguishes a priori arguments (from concept to existence — Anselm's ontological) from a posteriori arguments (from observation). His Five Ways are all a posteriori — they begin from empirical features of the world.

First Way (motion): things move; an unmoved mover is required. Second Way (efficient causation): a first cause is required. Third Way (contingency): contingent things require a necessary being. Fourth Way (degree): degrees of perfection require a maximum. Fifth Way (teleology): purposive ordering requires a designer.

Each has been criticised separately. Hume and Kant attacked the cosmological framework; Darwinian biology challenges the teleological reading; Russell's exchange with Copleston (1948 BBC debate) challenged the contingency argument.
items.why: Aquinas is sometimes reduced to a single 'cosmological argument'. He offered five distinct arguments that need to be evaluated separately — and Catholic natural theology still rests on this framework.

items.title: Paley's watchmaker argument was published in 1802

options.text: If we found a stone on a heath, we would infer no designer
If we found a watch on a heath, the complexity and purposive arrangement of its parts would compel us to infer a watchmaker — and similar reasoning applied to nature implies a divine designer
Nature is too random to need a designer
The argument compares the universe to a clockwork mechanism explicitly

items.reveal:
William Paley's 'Natural Theology' (1802) opens with the watch-on-the-heath analogy. He uses the human eye as his prime biological example.

Hume's 'Dialogues Concerning Natural Religion' (1779, published posthumously) anticipated and refuted versions of the design argument decades earlier — the analogy is weak (the universe is not like a watch), there are flaws (suggesting an apprentice designer or a committee), and the argument cannot reach a single benevolent God.

Darwin's 'On the Origin of Species' (1859) provided a non-design explanation for biological complexity. Modern Intelligent Design (Behe, Dembski, 1990s onwards) is a controversial attempt to revive the argument scientifically.
items.why: The design argument keeps returning in new forms. Each version has to deal with the next development in science — biological evolution, cosmic fine-tuning, multiverse cosmology — making it a moving target rather than a settled debate.

items.title: The Christian Bible's contents were not fixed until centuries after Christ
items.claim: When was the New Testament canon — the 27 books — first listed in its current form?

options.text: By the apostles themselves, before 70 CE
At the Council of Nicaea in 325 CE
Athanasius's Easter letter of 367 CE is the first surviving list of exactly the 27 books; consensus formed gradually through the 4th-5th centuries
By Pope Damasus I at the Council of Trent in 1546

items.reveal:
Athanasius of Alexandria's 39th Festal Letter (367 CE) is the first surviving document listing the 27 NT books we have today. Regional councils (Hippo 393, Carthage 397) confirmed it. The Trent council (1546) made it formal Catholic dogma — partly in response to the Reformation.

Nicaea (325) dealt with the Arian controversy, not the canon — a common confusion popularised by Dan Brown's 'The Da Vinci Code'.

Gospels left out include Thomas, Mary, Peter and the Infancy Gospel of James. Some books that nearly made it (the Shepherd of Hermas, 1 Clement) didn't.
items.why: The 'received text' image of Scripture obscures a long, contested human process. Knowing the canon was assembled doesn't disprove faith — but it changes the questions you can ask.
